lessons.title: Work done by constant forces
lessons.summary: Calculate signed work, identify zero work and use the correct displacement for a resistance or for weight.
lessons.objective: Calculate signed work, identify zero work and use the correct displacement for a resistance or for weight.
lessons.before: Mark the initial and final states and write out the quantities with their units.
lessons.ideas:
If the angle between force and displacement is \(\theta\), use \(W=Fd\cos\theta\). One joule is one newton metre.

Acute \(\theta\) gives positive work, a right angle gives zero, and obtuse \(\theta\) gives negative work.

For \(\theta=90^\circ\), \(\cos\theta=0\). For zero displacement, the work is zero regardless of the angle.

For constant resisting force magnitude \(R\) and length \(d\), its signed work is \(-Rd\), and the positive loss is \(Rd\).

\(W_g=-mg\Delta h\), with upwards positive. On a straight incline of length \(d\), the height gain uphill is \(d\sin\alpha\).
lessons.method:
1. Work describes the energy transferred by a force as its point of application moves. For a constant force and a straight displacement, resolve the force along the movement before multiplying by the distance.

  2. When the force has a component back against the displacement, that component does negative work. This can occur even when another force keeps the body moving forwards.

  3. A force does zero work if its point of application stays still, or if it acts perpendicular to the displacement. A normal force on a fixed smooth track is an important example.

  4. A resistance pointing back along the path does negative work. The phrase ‘work done against resistance’ asks for the corresponding positive amount of energy dissipated.

  5. Weight points downwards. Its work depends on the signed vertical displacement \(\Delta h\), even when the route is longer than that displacement.
mistakes: The angle must be measured from the actual displacement direction. An angle to a wall or a vertical axis may need to be converted.
Changing a work result to a positive number loses information about how the force transfers energy.
A large normal reaction does not transfer energy to a particle sliding along a fixed supporting surface.
Use the distance travelled while the resistance acts. A vertical rise or a horizontal projection does not give the resistive work on a slope.
For a downhill motion \(\Delta h<0\). Gravity then does positive work.

examples.title: Find signed work from an angle
examples.question: The sample carriage moves \(15\,\mathrm m\) in a straight line. A constant force has magnitude \(28\,\mathrm N\) at angle \(60^\circ\) to the displacement. Find the signed work done by that force.
examples.solution:
The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=14\) newtons.

Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=28\times 15\times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=210\).

The force does \(210\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is positive because the force partly helps the motion.

examples.title: Find signed work from an angle
examples.question: The sample carriage moves \(5\,\mathrm m\) in a straight line. A constant force has magnitude \(32\,\mathrm N\) at angle \(120^\circ\) to the displacement. Find the signed work done by that force.
examples.solution:
The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=-16\) newtons.

Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=32\times 5\times\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)=-80\).

The force does \(-80\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is negative because the force has a component opposing motion.

examples.title: Find signed work from an angle
examples.question: The measuring cart moves \(22\,\mathrm m\) in a straight line. A constant force has magnitude \(14\,\mathrm N\) at angle \(180^\circ\) to the displacement. Find the signed work done by that force.
examples.solution:
The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=-14\) newtons.

Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=14\times 22\times\left(-1\right)=-308\).

The force does \(-308\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is negative because the force has a component opposing motion.

examples.title: Find signed work from an angle
examples.question: The marker tray moves \(8\,\mathrm m\) in a straight line. A constant force has magnitude \(54\,\mathrm N\) at angle \(90^\circ\) to the displacement. Find the signed work done by that force.
examples.solution:
The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=0\) newtons.

Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=54\times 8\times\left(0\right)=0\).

The force does \(0\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is zero because there is no displacement along the force.

lessons.title: Kinetic and gravitational potential energy
lessons.summary: Calculate KE, recover speed and compare GPE relative to a consistent height datum.
lessons.objective: Calculate KE, recover speed and compare GPE relative to a consistent height datum.
lessons.before: Mark the initial and final states and write out the quantities with their units.
lessons.ideas:
\(K=\frac12mv^2\). Doubling the mass doubles \(K\) if speed is fixed. Doubling the speed multiplies \(K\) by four at fixed mass.

\(\Delta K=\frac12m(v^2-u^2)\), final energy minus initial energy.

\(v=\sqrt{\frac{2K}{m}}\) when the mass is positive.

\(U=mgh\) for a chosen height origin, and \(\Delta U=mg(h_2-h_1)\).

Use \(E=K+U=\frac12mv^2+mgh\). The mechanical energy can change when external work is done or energy is dissipated.
lessons.method:
1. Kinetic energy is the energy associated with motion. It is determined by speed, so reversing the direction at the same speed leaves the kinetic energy unchanged.

  2. The particle can have positive kinetic energy at both endpoints yet lose kinetic energy between them.

  3. Undo the kinetic energy formula by isolating the speed squared. Speed is a magnitude, so take the non-negative square root.

  4. Choose a height that is convenient to call zero. The GPE relative to that level may be negative, while the difference between two GPE values is the same for every choice of reference.

  5. At each position, compute kinetic energy from its speed and GPE from its height. Their sum is the mechanical energy relative to the chosen reference.
mistakes: Square the speed before multiplying by half the mass.
The expression \(\frac12m(v-u)^2\) gives neither the signed change nor, in general, its magnitude.
A negative velocity may describe direction on a chosen axis. A negative speed is impossible.
Use the same reference before and after. A descent lowers GPE even when both heights are positive.
An object at rest may still have non-zero GPE relative to the chosen level.

examples.title: Calculate kinetic energy
examples.question: A particle of mass \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves at \(9\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its kinetic energy.
examples.solution:
Square the speed before multiplying by half the mass.

\(K=\frac12\times 6\times 9^2=243\).

The kinetic energy is \(243\,\mathrm J\).

examples.title: Calculate a signed kinetic energy change
examples.question: A particle of mass \(5\,\mathrm{kg}\) changes its speed from \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its signed kinetic energy change.
examples.solution:
The initial and final kinetic energies are \(\frac{605}{2}\,\mathrm J\) and \(\frac{245}{2}\,\mathrm J\), respectively.

Change means final minus initial. The signed kinetic energy change is \(-180\,\mathrm J\).

examples.title: Calculate a signed kinetic energy change
examples.question: A particle of mass \(9\,\mathrm{kg}\) changes its speed from \(7\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its signed kinetic energy change.
examples.solution:
The initial and final kinetic energies are \(\frac{441}{2}\,\mathrm J\) and \(648\,\mathrm J\), respectively.

Change means final minus initial. The signed kinetic energy change is \(\frac{855}{2}\,\mathrm J\).

examples.title: Recover speed from kinetic energy
examples.question: A trolley has mass \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\) and kinetic energy \(100\,\mathrm J\). Find its exact speed.
examples.solution:
Isolate the square of speed. \(v^2=\frac{2K}{m}=25\).

Speed is non-negative. Its exact value is \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

lessons.title: Work–energy principle and conservation
lessons.summary: Balance KE, GPE, work by a driving force and dissipation at endpoints of smooth or rough motion.
lessons.objective: Balance KE, GPE, work by a driving force and dissipation at endpoints of smooth or rough motion.
lessons.before: Mark the initial and final states and write out the quantities with their units.
lessons.ideas:
With positive loss \(L\), use \(K_f+\Delta U=K_i+W_{\rm drive}-L\). This is equivalent to \(\Delta K\) equalling the net work when gravity is written as work instead.

A vertical drop \(h\) gives \(v^2=u^2+2gh\), when there are no other energy transfers and contact continues.

For constant resistance \(R\) over length \(d\), write \(L=Rd\). Enter \(mg\Delta h\) separately.

With weight as the only force with a perpendicular component, \(R=mg\cos\alpha\) and \(L=\mu Rd\).

Rearrange to find either \(L=K_i+W_{\rm drive}-\Delta U-K_f\) or \(W_{\rm drive}=\Delta K+\Delta U+L\).
lessons.method:
1. Decide which body or combination of bodies is the system. Include gravity through a signed GPE change, then include driving work and resistive loss separately.

  2. For motion on a fixed smooth surface with no drag, the normal reaction is perpendicular to the instantaneous motion. It does no work, so energy can give information about the endpoints without finding forces along the curve.

  3. Resistance transfers energy along the full distance travelled. Gravity still depends only on the vertical displacement of the particle.

  4. For a particle sliding along a straight rough plane in this model, first obtain the normal reaction from the perpendicular forces. Then use the sliding friction magnitude and path length.

  5. When both endpoint speeds are known, evaluate both kinetic energies. The remaining change in GPE and known work terms can then isolate the missing contribution.
mistakes: Do not include gravity as work and also include it as GPE change in the same equation.
The energy method gives speed. It does not determine time or the changing normal reaction.
Using the slope length for the change in GPE, or the height change for friction, mixes different physical quantities.
If an applied force presses into the plane or lifts partly off it, the normal reaction changes.
An energy loss written as a positive amount cannot be negative. If a result has that sign, review the data and direction convention.

examples.title: Find a speed using an energy balance
examples.question: A trial pod of mass \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\) enters a track at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It rises by \(3\,\mathrm m\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). A driving force transfers \(200\,\mathrm J\) of energy to it. Resistive forces dissipate \(46\,\mathrm J\). Find the exact speed at the end.
examples.solution:
Use \(K_f+\Delta U=K_i+W_{\rm drive}-L\), where \(L\) is the positive amount dissipated.

The initial kinetic energy is \(48\,\mathrm J\) and the signed potential energy change is \(180\,\mathrm J\).

Substituting the work and the potential energy change gives \(K_f=22\) joules.

The final kinetic energy is \(22\,\mathrm J\), so the exact final speed is \(\frac{\sqrt{66}}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find speed on a smooth curved track
examples.question: A particle enters a smooth curved track at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It remains in contact and reaches a point \(\frac{5}{2}\,\mathrm m\) vertically below the entry. Neglect drag. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its exact speed at this point.
examples.solution:
The normal force is perpendicular to the instantaneous movement. It does no work, and no energy is dissipated.

The loss of gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy.

\(v^2=u^2+2gh=66\), where \(h\) is the vertical drop. The exact speed is \(\sqrt{66}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

examples.title: Find the height reached when speed becomes zero
examples.question: A particle starts up a smooth track at \(11\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It remains in contact until it reaches its turning point. Neglect air resistance. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find its maximum vertical rise.
examples.solution:
At the turning point, the speed is zero. Initial kinetic energy becomes a gain in GPE.

\(\frac12mu^2=mgh\), so \(h=\frac{u^2}{2g}=\frac{121}{20}\).

The maximum vertical rise is \(\frac{121}{20}\,\mathrm m\).

examples.title: Use friction distance separately from height
examples.question: A sled of mass \(7\,\mathrm{kg}\) enters a straight section at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It travels \(21\,\mathrm m\) along the section and descends by \(5\,\mathrm m\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). A constant resistance of \(8\,\mathrm N\) opposes the movement. Find its exact exit speed.
examples.solution:
The path length belongs in resistive work. The height change belongs in gravitational potential energy.

Write \(\frac12mv^2=56-\left(-350\right)-Rd\).

The final kinetic energy is \(238\,\mathrm J\), so its exact exit speed is \(2 \sqrt{17}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

lessons.title: Energy across stages and connected particles
lessons.summary: Track energy through changes of surface, stopping and return journeys, and use a combined system for connected particles.
lessons.objective: Track energy through changes of surface, stopping and return journeys, and use a combined system for connected particles.
lessons.before: Mark the initial and final states and write out the quantities with their units.
lessons.ideas:
At a boundary without an impact or stated loss, the last kinetic energy of the earlier stage becomes the first of the next stage.

On a level unpowered section with constant resistance, \(R=\frac{K_{\rm entry}-K_{\rm exit}}{d}\).

On a level run with constant resistance, \(d=\frac{K_{\rm entry}}R\) until speed reaches zero.

For a round trip over the same distance \(d\) each way with constant resistance magnitude, the loss is \(2Rd\). The final GPE relative to the start is unchanged.

Add both kinetic energies and both signed GPE changes. A rise and fall of equal length do not imply equal energy changes if the masses differ.
lessons.method:
1. Split the route at boundaries where a different force acts, the resistance changes or an intermediate speed is requested. A stage can otherwise be treated as one energy balance.

  2. Calculate the kinetic energy entering the later section. Use the known final speed to calculate the remaining kinetic energy. The difference tells you what was transferred out on that section, after accounting for any work or height change.

  3. The motion may continue after leaving a slope. Find the kinetic energy at the bottom, then use the new resistance to determine the distance before the first stop.

  4. If a particle reverses direction, friction reverses too. Friction opposes the movement on both legs and transfers mechanical energy away on each one.

  5. When a light taut string runs over a smooth pulley, its tension does positive work on one particle and equal negative work on the other for equal displacements. Its net contribution cancels if both particles are included in the system.
mistakes: Do not reuse the original speed at a later boundary. Calculate the boundary speed or carry its kinetic energy forwards.
Do not divide a total-route loss by the distance of just one stage.
That stopping distance is measured from the start of the run. Add the earlier slope length only if total route length is requested.
Zero overall displacement does not imply zero resistive work. Each leg has its own displacement and resistance direction.
Do not cancel the tension work if analysing just one particle.

examples.title: Carry kinetic energy between two stages
examples.question: A rail cart of mass \(6\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves from \(A\) at \(4\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Straight section \(AB\) is \(15\,\mathrm m\) long and drops vertically by \(3\,\mathrm m\). Its constant resistance is \(7\,\mathrm N\). The following level stretch \(BC\) is \(9\,\mathrm m\) long, with no energy lost at the transition. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Its constant resistance on \(BC\) is \(5\,\mathrm N\). Find the exact speeds at \(B\) and \(C\).
examples.solution:
For \(AB\), gravity releases \(180\,\mathrm J\) and resistance dissipates \(105\,\mathrm J\).

The kinetic energy at \(B\) is \(K_B=48+180-105=123\) joules, giving speed \(\sqrt{41}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

On \(BC\), there is no GPE change. The energy loss is \(45\,\mathrm J\), leaving \(78\,\mathrm J\).

The speeds are \(\sqrt{41}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(B\) and \(\sqrt{26}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at \(C\).

examples.title: Carry kinetic energy between two stages
examples.question: A rail cart of mass \(9\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves from \(A\) at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Straight section \(AB\) is \(12\,\mathrm m\) long and drops vertically by \(4\,\mathrm m\). Its constant resistance is \(7\,\mathrm N\). The following level stretch \(BC\) is \(15\,\mathrm m\) long, with no energy lost at the transition. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The cart leaves \(C\) at exact speed \(\frac{\sqrt{393}}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its exact speed at \(B\) and the constant resistance on \(BC\).
examples.solution:
For \(AB\), gravity releases \(360\,\mathrm J\) and resistance dissipates \(84\,\mathrm J\).

The kinetic energy at \(B\) is \(K_B=\frac{81}{2}+360-84=\frac{633}{2}\) joules, giving speed \(\frac{\sqrt{633}}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

On \(BC\), there is no GPE change. The given final speed gives \(\frac{393}{2}\,\mathrm J\) of kinetic energy.

The speed at \(B\) is \(\frac{\sqrt{633}}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the resistance on \(BC\) is \(R_2=\frac{K_B-K_C}{d_2}=8\) newtons.

examples.title: Carry kinetic energy between two stages
examples.question: A rail cart of mass \(12\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves from \(A\) at \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Straight section \(AB\) is \(12\,\mathrm m\) long and drops vertically by \(3\,\mathrm m\). Its constant resistance is \(12\,\mathrm N\). The following level stretch \(BC\) is \(14\,\mathrm m\) long, with no energy lost at the transition. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). The cart leaves \(C\) at exact speed \(\frac{\sqrt{381}}{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). Find its exact speed at \(B\) and the constant resistance on \(BC\).
examples.solution:
For \(AB\), gravity releases \(360\,\mathrm J\) and resistance dissipates \(144\,\mathrm J\).

The kinetic energy at \(B\) is \(K_B=150+360-144=366\) joules, giving speed \(\sqrt{61}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

On \(BC\), there is no GPE change. The given final speed gives \(254\,\mathrm J\) of kinetic energy.

The speed at \(B\) is \(\sqrt{61}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the resistance on \(BC\) is \(R_2=\frac{K_B-K_C}{d_2}=8\) newtons.

examples.title: Find the level stopping distance after a descent
examples.question: A sled of mass \(8\,\mathrm{kg}\) enters a straight slope at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The slope length is \(15\,\mathrm m\), with vertical drop \(4\,\mathrm m\) and constant resistance \(9\,\mathrm N\). It then travels onto a level run with constant resistance \(18\,\mathrm N\), retaining its speed as it enters the run. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). How far does it travel on the level run before first coming to rest?
examples.solution:
Find the energy at the foot of the incline. It is the initial kinetic energy plus gravitational energy released, minus the work against the first resistance.

This leaves \(K_B=36+320-135=221\) joules.

On the level part the height is constant. The resistance does work against the remaining kinetic energy until the sled stops.

\(d=\frac{K_B}{R_2}=\frac{221}{18}\). The level stopping distance is \(\frac{221}{18}\,\mathrm m\).

lessons.title: Average power, driving force and acceleration
lessons.summary: Distinguish average and instantaneous power. Link driving force to power on level and sloping roads.
lessons.objective: Distinguish average and instantaneous power. Link driving force to power on level and sloping roads.
lessons.before: Mark the initial and final states and write out the quantities with their units.
lessons.ideas:
\(P_{\rm avg}=\frac{W}{t}\). A watt is a joule per second and \(1\,\mathrm{kW}=1000\,\mathrm W\).

For forward driving, \(P=Fv\). Use \(F=\frac Pv\) when \(v>0\). At fixed power a faster vehicle has a smaller driving force.

With positive direction along motion, use \(F=R+mg\sin\alpha\) uphill and \(F=R-mg\sin\alpha\) downhill when the engine still drives forward.

Along the motion, \(ma=F-R-mg\sin\alpha\) uphill. Determine \(F\) from \(P\) and \(v\) before substituting.

Uphill at speed \(v\), GPE increases at rate \(mgv\sin\alpha\) and resistive loss is \(Rv\).
lessons.method:
1. Work is an amount of energy transferred. Power states how fast that work is done. A fixed amount of work completed sooner has a greater average power.

  2. If a force acts along the motion, its instantaneous power is the force magnitude times the speed. The engine’s power therefore gives the engine force at a known speed.

  3. At steady speed the resultant along the road is zero. Uphill, the engine balances resistance and the slope component of weight. Downhill, gravity assists the engine against resistance.

  4. Use the actual speed at the specified instant to obtain the driving force. Then use the signed force equation along the road. The result can be negative even when the vehicle is moving forwards.

  5. At steady speed the rate of gain of kinetic energy is zero. The engine may still be raising the height and replacing energy dissipated by resistance.
mistakes: Convert minutes to seconds first. Do not divide energy in joules by time in minutes and label the result as watts.
The engine force differs from the resultant force whenever there is resistance or a component of weight along the road.
The same power need not produce the same steady speed on a hill and a level road.
Setting the resultant to zero assumes steady speed. That assumption is invalid when acceleration is requested.
Zero acceleration does not imply zero engine power. It says that the kinetic energy stays constant.

examples.title: Use work and elapsed time
examples.question: A motor does \(36\,\mathrm{kJ}\) of work in \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{min}\). Find its average power in watts.
examples.solution:
Convert to joules and seconds: \(36000\,\mathrm J\) in \(90\,\mathrm s\). Divide work by time.

Use \(P_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{W}{t}\). This relates an entire interval to one average value.

The average power is \(400\,\mathrm{W}\).

examples.title: Link engine power and the driving force
examples.question: A carrier moves at \(15\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at a given instant. Its engine exerts a driving force of \(640\,\mathrm N\) in the direction of motion. Find the instantaneous power.
examples.solution:
At the stated instant and with force aligned with motion, use \(P=Fv\).

The engine power is \(P=640\times 15=9600\) watts.

examples.title: Link engine power and the driving force
examples.question: A carrier moves at \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at a given instant. Its engine develops \(\frac{58}{5}\,\mathrm{kW}\). The driving force acts in the direction of motion. Find its magnitude.
examples.solution:
Convert the engine output to \(11600\,\mathrm W\).

Use \(F=\frac{P}{v}=725\). The driving force is \(725\,\mathrm N\).

examples.title: Find steady speed or instantaneous acceleration
examples.question: A small vehicle of mass \(1000\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves straight uphill along a road whose sine of inclination is \(\frac{1}{20}\). A constant resistance of \(360\,\mathrm N\) acts against the motion. The engine supplies \(\frac{86}{5}\,\mathrm{kW}\) in the direction of motion. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the steady speed when this power is maintained.
examples.solution:
At steady speed the force resultant along the road is zero. Weight contributes a signed opposition of \(500\,\mathrm N\) and resistance contributes \(360\,\mathrm N\).

Balance forces to give engine driving force \(860\,\mathrm N\).

Use \(v=\frac{P}{F}=20\). The steady speed is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

The force component along the displacement is \(F\cos\theta=\frac{35}{2}\) newtons.

Multiply the signed component by the distance. \(W=35\times 18\times\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=315\).

The force does \(315\,\mathrm J\) of work. This is positive because the force partly helps the motion.

questions.title: Distinguish work by and against a resistance
questions.prompt_html: A cart moves \(41\,\mathrm m\) against a constant resistance of \(19\,\mathrm N\). Find the signed work done by resistance and the energy lost to resistance.
questions.answer_html: Resistance does \(-779\,\mathrm J\) of work. The amount of energy transferred away from mechanical energy is \(779\,\mathrm J\).
questions.solution_html:
The force points opposite to the displacement, so its own work is \(-Rd\).

The product of the two magnitudes is \(779\,\mathrm J\).

Resistance does \(-779\,\mathrm J\) of work. The amount of energy transferred away from mechanical energy is \(779\,\mathrm J\).

questions.title: Calculate work by weight on a slope
questions.prompt_html: A particle, modelled as a instrument sled, has mass \(11\,\mathrm{kg}\) moves \(25\,\mathrm m\) up a slope. The sine of the inclination is \(\frac{7}{25}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Give its signed height change (upwards positive) and the work done by gravity.
questions.answer_html: The height change is \(7\,\mathrm m\) and work done by gravity is \(-770\,\mathrm J\).

A particle enters a smooth curved track at a height of \(6\,\mathrm m\) above a datum and at \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). It remains in contact. Resistive forces are negligible. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find the exact speed at a point \(2\,\mathrm m\) above the datum. [2]

  2. The track continues to rise until the particle comes momentarily to rest. Find this height above the datum. Explain why the shape of the intervening track is not needed. [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) \(v^2=u^2+2gh=89\), where \(h\) is the vertical drop. The exact speed is \(\sqrt{89}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(b) The height is \(\frac{129}{20}\,\mathrm m\) above the datum, determined by the endpoint states.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The normal force is perpendicular to the instantaneous movement. It does no work, and no energy is dissipated.

The loss of gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy.

\(v^2=u^2+2gh=89\), where \(h\) is the vertical drop. The exact speed is \(\sqrt{89}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Part (b)

At rest, \(\frac12m(3^2)+mg(6)=mgh_{\max}\), so \(h_{\max}=6+\frac9{20}=\frac{129}{20}\,\mathrm m\).

Normal reaction does no work, leaving gravity as the only force doing work. Its work depends only on the vertical difference.

The height is \(\frac{129}{20}\,\mathrm m\) above the datum, determined by the endpoint states.
questions.hint_html: The vertical drop to the low point is four metres. For the turning height, return to the original energy state.

questions.title: Find the engine work from readings
questions.prompt_html:
A \(4\,\mathrm{kg}\) track unit runs for \(15\,\mathrm m\) up a straight track, rising \(3\,\mathrm m\). The speed changes from \(3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) to \(5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and resistance dissipates \(70\,\mathrm J\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find the signed changes in kinetic and potential energy. [2]

  2. Find the work done by the engine and hence its constant driving force acting along the track. [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) The GPE change is \(4\times10\times3=120\,\mathrm J\). Both changes are positive.

(b) The force is along the displacement, so \(F=\frac{222}{15}=\frac{74}{5}\,\mathrm N\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The KE change is \(\frac12(4)(5^2-3^2)=32\,\mathrm J\).

The GPE change is \(4\times10\times3=120\,\mathrm J\). Both changes are positive.

Part (b)

The engine supplies both increases and replaces the loss: \(W=32+120+70=222\,\mathrm J\).

The force is along the displacement, so \(F=\frac{222}{15}=\frac{74}{5}\,\mathrm N\).

The kinetic energy at the start of the level run is \(64+240-120=184\,\mathrm J\).

A constant resistance of \(320\,\mathrm N\) acts against the motion. The engine supplies \(\frac{324}{25}\,\mathrm{kW}\) in the direction of motion. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Find the driving force and the signed acceleration at the instant its speed is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The direction of motion is positive.
questions.answer_html: The driving force is \(648\,\mathrm N\) and signed acceleration is \(- \frac{3}{35}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
questions.solution_html:
Find the driving force from \(F=\frac{P}{v}=648\) newtons.

The opposition to forward motion is \(320\,\mathrm N\) from resistance plus \(400\,\mathrm N\) as the signed weight contribution.

Newton’s second law along the motion gives \(ma=648-\left(720\right)\).

The driving force is \(648\,\mathrm N\) and signed acceleration is \(- \frac{3}{35}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
questions.hint_html: Calculate the driving force from power first if speed is known. Keep the weight component, resistance and driving force separate.

questions.title: An average over two durations
questions.prompt_html:
A winch develops \(27\,\mathrm{kW}\) for \(18\,\mathrm s\), then \(14\,\mathrm{kW}\) for \(32\,\mathrm s\). Each power is constant during its own interval.

  1. Calculate the total work done in joules. [2]

  2. Find the average power in kilowatts over the whole operation. Explain why the arithmetic mean of the two powers is unsuitable. [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) The total work is \(27000(18)+14000(32)=934000\,\mathrm J\).

(b) The average is \(18.68\,\mathrm{kW}\). The two stages last different lengths of time, so their powers do not carry equal weight.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The work in each interval is power in watts times time in seconds.

The total work is \(27000(18)+14000(32)=934000\,\mathrm J\).

Part (b)

The full time is \(50\,\mathrm s\), so \(P_{\rm avg}=\frac{934000}{50}=18680\,\mathrm W\).

The average is \(18.68\,\mathrm{kW}\). The two stages last different lengths of time, so their powers do not carry equal weight.
questions.hint_html: Find work for each stage before combining the stages.

questions.title: Steady speed and a different moment on a slope
questions.prompt_html:
An \(840\,\mathrm{kg}\) vehicle travels uphill along the steepest line. The sine of the slope angle is \(\frac1{21}\) and the resistance is \(320\,\mathrm N\). The engine develops \(14.4\,\mathrm{kW}\). Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find the steady speed at this power. [3]

  2. At a different instant the speed is \(16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) at the same power. Find the signed acceleration, taking uphill as positive. [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) Use \(v=\frac{P}{F}=20\). The steady speed is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

(b) The driving force is \(900\,\mathrm N\) and signed acceleration is \(\frac{3}{14}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At steady speed the force resultant along the road is zero. Weight contributes a signed opposition of \(400\,\mathrm N\) and resistance contributes \(320\,\mathrm N\).

Balance forces to give engine driving force \(720\,\mathrm N\).

Use \(v=\frac{P}{F}=20\). The steady speed is \(20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\).

Part (b)

Find the driving force from \(F=\frac{P}{v}=900\) newtons.

The opposition to forward motion is \(320\,\mathrm N\) from resistance plus \(400\,\mathrm N\) as the signed weight contribution.

Newton’s second law along the motion gives \(ma=900-\left(720\right)\).

The driving force is \(900\,\mathrm N\) and signed acceleration is \(\frac{3}{14}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).
questions.hint_html: The engine force at sixteen metres per second is different from the engine force at steady speed.

questions.title: Gravity supplies some of the power downhill
questions.prompt_html:
A \(750\,\mathrm{kg}\) track vehicle descends steadily at \(12\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The slope has sine \(\frac1{30}\). The opposition due to resistance is \(700\,\mathrm N\) and the engine drives forward. Take \(g=10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\).

  1. Find the power of the engine and the rate at which resistance dissipates energy. [3]

  2. The engine is switched off while the vehicle still has the same speed. Find its acceleration at that instant, with downhill taken as positive. [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) Engine power is \(450(12)=5400\,\mathrm W\), and resistive dissipation has rate \(700(12)=8400\,\mathrm W\). The difference is supplied by loss of GPE.

(b) The signed acceleration is \(\frac{-450}{750}=-\frac35\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), so the vehicle slows as it moves downhill.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The forward component of weight is \(750(10)\frac1{30}=250\,\mathrm N\). At steady speed the engine supplies the remainder \(700-250=450\,\mathrm N\).

Engine power is \(450(12)=5400\,\mathrm W\), and resistive dissipation has rate \(700(12)=8400\,\mathrm W\). The difference is supplied by loss of GPE.

Part (b)

The force resultant immediately becomes \(250-700=-450\,\mathrm N\).

The signed acceleration is \(\frac{-450}{750}=-\frac35\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), so the vehicle slows as it moves downhill.
questions.hint_html: Gravity helps the downhill movement. The power dissipated need not equal engine power.
